5. Historical Data Collection

Observed data are based on in situ instrumental measurements of water temperature worldwide. When paired with appropriate screening criteria and bias correction algorithms, in situ records provide a reliable long-term record of temperature. The long-term sampling was not based on a scientific sampling design but was gathered by “ships of opportunity” and other ad hoc records. Observations from drifting and moored buoys began to be added in the late 1970s. The most recent version of ERSST, version 5, includes data from the Argo array network of free-drifting floats, which began to be deployed in 2000 and now number close to 4,000 floats throughout the world’s oceans. The technical documentation for the Sea Surface Temperature indicator provides more details about these different measurement methods, with links to additional information about their sampling and analytical procedures and their relative availability, coverage, accuracy, and biases. The indicator’s documentation also explains why ERSST.v5 excludes satellite data.

6. Indicator Derivation

Observed Data

NOAA’s ERSST reconstruction involves filtering and blending data sets that use alternative measurement methods and include redundancies in space and time. Because of these redundancies, this reconstruction is able to fill spatial and temporal data gaps and correct for biases in the different measurement techniques (e.g., uninsulated canvas buckets, intakes near warm engines, uneven spatial coverage). Locations have been combined to report a single global value, based on scientifically valid techniques for averaging over areas. Specifically, data have been averaged over 2-by-2-degree grid cells. Daily and monthly records have been averaged to find annual anomalies. The technical documentation for EPA’s Sea Surface Temperature indicator provides additional discussion of reconstruction methods, along with links to published methodology papers.

This figure shows the extended reconstructed data as anomalies, or differences, from a baseline “climate normal.” In this case, the climate normal was defined to be the average SST from 1971 to 2000.

Model Outputs

The project team performed the following steps via R scripts:

  • For each model, and each year, the team averaged the “tos” variable over all months of the year at each grid cell.
  • The team calculated the 1971–2000 average for each pixel using the model hindcast, then calculated each future year’s anomaly relative to this historical baseline.
  • The team calculated a global mean anomaly for each year, using the CMIP6 variable “areacello” to represent the proper area of each grid cell, as cell area varies with latitude.
  • In performing these calculations, the team also applied a coastline mask to ensure that mixed land/ocean pixels were included in the analysis as only partial (ocean) pixels and weighted accordingly.
  • The team converted from Celsius to Fahrenheit.
  • The team aggregated the 16 models using the standard Bayesian model weighting approach used in the Fifth National Climate Assessment and documented by Massoud et al. (2023).
  • The team smoothed modeled results using an 11-year moving average. The team performed this step independently for the hindcast (through 2014) and for each scenario from 2015 (the first year of divergence) forward.

7. Alignment

To ensure consistency in how SST anomalies are defined, the project team had to ensure that the observed and modeled anomalies were all presented relative to a common baseline. The observed CONUS anomalies for the graph had already been calculated with respect to a 1971–2000 baseline, as shown in the Sea Surface Temperature indicator. Thus, the project team also calculated model anomalies relative to the hindcast’s 1971–2000 baseline. The results show good alignment, so no transformation was necessary.

8. Display

The interactive graph for this pairing shows the following elements:

  • Observed data from 1880 to 2023.
  • Modeled hindcast from 1880 to 2014. The line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted from 1885 to 2009, as the project team did not attempt to apply any endpoint padding at either end of the series.
  • Modeled projections from 2015 to 2100 for four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, and SSP5-8.5), with 2014 added for continuity (2014 is the last year before the scenarios diverge). Each scenario line on the graph shows the Bayesian weighted average of the 16 GCMs, smoothed using an 11-year moving average. The resulting 11-year means are plotted starting at 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast annual ranges, although the scenarios do not start to diverge until 2015. Smoothed values for 2014–2019 pick up some hindcast years in the average. The 11-year means are plotted through 2095, including data from 2090 through 2100, the last year of available data. Scenarios have been assigned “plain-language” names for consistency throughout this pairings effort.
  • A shaded band around each of the scenarios reflects the 10th to 90th percentiles among the 16 models. This shaded band therefore illustrates the range of modeled values. The shaded bands show annual values; they have not been smoothed. The projected ranges start in 2014 to provide continuity with the hindcast, but the scenarios begin to diverge in 2015.

9. Quality Assurance and Quality Control

For observed data, thorough documentation of quality assurance and quality control methods and results is available in the technical references for ERSST.v5. Quality procedures for each GCM (e.g., validation) are described in source papers published by the organizations that have developed and run each model; these sources are available through the links in the overall technical documentation [to be linked] for this effort. For each pairing, the project team conducted typical quality control steps, including independently checking all aggregations, unit conversions, transformations, and other calculations.
